title: Deployment of Entanglement-Based QKD in Financial Infrastructure
authors: Mirela Selimović, Roman Solar, Jonathan Gruner, Sebastian Mair, Mario Wenzl, Thomas Heine, Matej Pivoluska, Rupert Ursin, Sebastian Philipp Neumann
abstract: We demonstrate the feasibility of entanglement-based quantum key distribution (eQKD) in high-security financial infrastructure over a 22 km fiber link with 8 dB loss between two data centers using polarization entanglement. The fully automated system continuously generated secure keys for four months at an average rate of 63.8 kb/s, which were stored into a key management system and consumed to establish a VPN tunnel. The setup achieved 93.7% total up-time, with no downtime caused by the quantum optical components. Active polarization control kept the quantum bit error rate below 2% for 97.4% of the time and timing synchronization based on the entangled photon pairs' intrinsic temporal correlations achieved sub-300 ps precision. Our standalone system requires neither polarized guide lasers nor external high-precision time references. These results show practical integration of eQKD into operational financial infrastructure.
summary: The paper reports on the successful real-world implementation of entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution (eQKD) over a 22 km fiber link connecting two data centers. By integrating active polarization control and robust error correction protocols, the system maintained high key generation rates and uptime for months. This demonstrates a significant step toward deploying quantum security measures in commercial financial infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary goal was demonstrating the practical feasibility of entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution (eQKD) within a high-security, real-world financial data center infrastructure.
main_result: The system successfully achieved stable key generation rates (average 63.8 kb/s) and maintained high uptime (93.7%) over four months of continuous operation on a 22 km fiber link.
method: The authors employed the BBM92 protocol using polarization-entangled photon pairs generated via SPDC, incorporating active feedback loops for polarization drift compensation and advanced post-processing techniques like LDPC error correction and privacy amplification.
model_or_system: The physical platform is an eQKD system transmitting quantum states over a 22 km standard optical fiber link between two data centers. Key components include Polarization Analysis Modules (PAMs), superconducting detectors, and active polarization controllers that compensate for environmental birefringence changes.
key_observables: Average secure key rate ($\approx 63.8$ kb/s); Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) maintained below $2\%$ for over $97\%$ of the time; Timing precision achieved was sub-300 ps.
important_parameters: Fiber loss of 8 dB over 22 km; Operational duration of four months; QBER threshold used for control ($\ge 2\%$).
main_assumptions: The system relies on active polarization control to counteract environmental perturbations, and the post-processing framework assumes certain efficiencies (e.g., equal detection efficiencies in both bases).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the point-to-point setup schematic, showing key rate stability over months, QBER evolution with compensation activity, and relative clock drift measurements over extended periods.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup (source, transmission link), describes the measurement protocols (basis choice, timing synchronization), outlines the complex post-processing chain (PE, EC via LDPC, PA), presents long-term performance data, and concludes with integration results into a live network environment.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete engineering demonstration of quantum key distribution outside of controlled lab settings, directly addressing the deployment challenges for quantum technologies in critical infrastructure.

FIG. 3: Polarization rotation over a full day of operation in deployed fiber link. The top panel shows the quantum bit error rate (QBER) as a function of time over one typical day of operation. Shaded regions indicate intervals where the QBER drifted in a favorable direction without intervention, while dashed lines mark instances where the polarization control algorithm is initiated to actively reduce the QBER. The algorithm is initiated once the QBER reaches ≥2 % (black horizontal line). The bottom panel displays the corresponding evolution of the three input voltages ϕ1, ϕ2 and ϕ3 of the polarization controller.

FIG. 4: Relative clock drift rate over four months of continuous operation. The graph shows the relative time drift rate, τ (µs/s), over the course of operation, resulting from the independent drift of the time-tagging clocks. The inset plot shows the coincidence count rate over two days of operation (red shaded region in main plot). Whenever the time drift reaches 500 µs, a re-synchronization event is initiated, resulting in a higher coincidence count rate and a sawtooth pattern.
